content: 1. Daily iron supplementation is recommended for menstruating women living in areas with a high prevalence of anemia. This intervention aims to improve hemoglobin levels, enhance iron status, and reduce the risk of anemia in populations where anemia affects 20% or more of non-pregnant women of reproductive age. 2. Daily iron supplementation is also recommended for school-age children aged 60 months and older in settings with a high prevalence of anemia. This measure is intended to prevent iron deficiency and anemia. 3. In malaria-endemic areas, iron supplementation for infants and children should be provided alongside public health measures to prevent, diagnose, and treat malaria. 4. Intermittent iron supplementation is recommended for preschool and school-age children in areas where anemia prevalence is 20% or higher. This approach aims to improve iron status and reduce the risk of anemia. 5. Postpartum women may be provided with oral iron supplementation, either alone or in combination with folic acid, for 6–12 weeks after delivery. This is recommended in settings where gestational anemia is a public health concern to reduce the risk of postpartum anemia. 6. Routine use of multiple micronutrient powders during pregnancy is not recommended as a substitute for standard iron and folic acid supplementation. This is because it does not improve maternal and infant health outcomes effectively. 7. Vitamin A supplementation for postpartum women is not recommended for preventing maternal and infant morbidity and mortality. 8. Anemia in individuals diagnosed with the condition should be treated according to national guidelines. 9. Undernutrition in adolescents can manifest as severe acute malnutrition or micronutrient-related deficiencies. This condition limits growth, weakens the immune system, and impairs the body’s ability to recover from injuries or illnesses. 10. Adolescents with severe acute malnutrition should be identified, assessed, and managed according to WHO guidelines. Community engagement is essential for follow-up and support in such cases. 11. In humanitarian and fragile settings, it is critical to assess conditions and ensure adequate nutritional provisions for adolescents, considering their age, gender, weight, and activity levels. 12. Adolescents presenting with weight loss should be assessed for underlying causes and managed accordingly. Nutritional counseling and support should be provided, and at-risk adolescents should be enrolled in programs offering nutritional assessment and care. 13. All individuals, including those with tuberculosis or other infections, require a balanced diet containing essential macroand micronutrients for optimal health and recovery. 14. Patients with active tuberculosis and severe acute malnutrition should be treated in line with WHO recommendations for managing severe acute malnutrition. 15. Patients with active tuberculosis and moderate undernutrition who fail to regain normal BMI after two months of treatment, or who lose weight during treatment, should be evaluated for adherence and comorbid conditions. Nutritional assessment and counseling should be provided, and nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods should be offered as needed. 16. Pregnant women with active tuberculosis and moderate undernutrition, or those with inadequate weight gain, should receive nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods to achieve a minimum weekly weight gain of approximately 300 grams during the second and third trimesters. 17. Patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and moderate undernutrition should also be provided with nutrient-rich or fortified supplementary foods to restore normal nutritional status. 18. Preventing adolescent pregnancy and poor reproductive outcomes requires universal access to sexual and reproductive health care. This includes contraception, antenatal care, and safe abortion services. 19. Globally, the adolescent birth rate among females aged 15–19 years declined by 21% from 2000 to 2015. However, it remains high in two-thirds of countries, with more than 20 births per 1,000 adolescent girls in 2015. 20. Maternal conditions, including hemorrhage, sepsis, hypertensive disorders, obstructed labor, and complications of abortion, are leading causes of death among adolescent girls aged 15–19 years. Adolescents are five times more likely to die during pregnancy and childbirth compared to adult women. 21. Complications of adolescent pregnancy include fetal growth retardation, preterm delivery, low birth weight, pre-eclampsia, cephalopelvic disproportion, stillbirth, and neonatal death. 22. Interventions to empower girls and support communities in delaying marriage and pregnancy are critical for reducing maternal mortality and complications from pregnancy and childbirth. 23. Efforts to reduce child marriage and coerced sex should include laws and policies prohibiting these practices, as well as community-based interventions to influence social norms. 24. Adolescents should have access to high-quality contraceptive information and services, including emergency contraception. Efforts should also be made to reduce the financial cost of contraceptives for adolescents. 25. Interventions should be implemented to improve adolescents’ access to safe abortion services, including informing them about the dangers of unsafe abortion methods and the availability of legal, safe abortion services. 26. Laws and policies should be enforced to punish perpetrators of coerced sex involving adolescent girls. Interventions should also focus on building adolescent girls’ self-esteem, life skills, and social support networks to help them resist and recover from coerced sex. 27. Interventions should engage men and boys in critically assessing gender norms and behaviors related to sexual coercion and violence, while also addressing broader social norms on these issues.
